newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate drops to 7-year low 5.1 percent.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate drops to 7-year low 5.1 percent.

text.p: The nation's jobless rate fell to a seven-year low of 5.1 percent last month from 5.4 percent in July as a bustling economy spawned broad-based job growth and higher wages, the government said Friday.

The report, the government's first assessment of the economy for August, was welcomed as a confirmation of economic vigour by the Clinton administration but seen by many private economists as an ominous sign of a tightening labour market on the verge of touching off an inflationary surge.

However, after a moment of uncertainty, financial markets rose on the news as stock and bond traders realised that the report did not point to a worse-than-predicted doomsday scenario of an overheating economy that many had expected.
The Dow Jones industrial average was up 54 points at 5,661 in late trading.

The economy created 250,000 non-farm jobs in August -- slightly more than economists had predicted and above the past year's monthly average of 211,100 -- after 228,000 were added to payrolls in July, the Labour Department said.
"I would say that the forward momentum of the economy is very strong," said economist Sam Kahan of ASK Investment Advisors in Chicago.

Many economists believe the current rate of job growth cannot be sustained without threatening to trigger inflation, which they said could prompt Federal Reserve policymakers to pre-emptively raise interest rates at their Sept. 24 meeting.
"If the economic numbers do not show consisderable weakness over the next two weeks, then the odds are pretty high that the Fed will tighten," said Kahan.

With a very high 63.3 percent of the working-age population employed last month, economists said the job market has taken in most available workers and may have to bid up wages to fill additional jobs, especially in many specialised occupations.

"It's not really rocket science here, we're running out of warm bodies," said economist Russ Sheldon of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh. "I think a reasonable person would view us in the zone of full employment already."

Indeed, the department said average hourly earnings rose 6 cents last month to $11.87 after falling 2 cents in July. Over the past year, hourly earnings rose 3.6 percent, outpacing the 3 percent gain in consumer prices over the same period.
But Labour Secretary Robert Reich said that, despite the strong numbers, there was still some "give" in labour markets.

"Let me assure financial markets, if I may, I still do not see any signs of wages pushing on inflation," he said in an interview on Reuters Financial Television. "The economy is percolating, but it is not boiling over."

On a campaign trip to Florida, President Bill Clinton said the report was evidence of strong growth and high consumer confidence and declared, "The American economy, my fellow Americans, is on the right track."

The decline in the unemployment rate, which was especially steep among workers over 55 years old and in their early 20s, brought the jobless rate to its lowest level since March 1989, when it was 5 percent, the department said.
Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics, attributed some of decline to seasonal distortions caused by the timing of its household survey.

Economists once thought that an unemployment rate below a so-called natural rate of 6 percent would push prices up. But the rate has been below that level for two years without any clear evidence of wage-driven inflation.

A survey by the 600,000-member Nation Federation of Independent Business found that 27 percent of small business owners raised workers' compensation recently, 20 percent plan to do so and a record 29 percent had trouble filling openings.
"The interesting question is where do you get the people?" said economist William Dunkelberg, who conducted the survey.

Of the 250,000 jobs created last month, 77,000 were in local government, mostly in schools, and another 81,000 were in an array of services, in particular business, temporary help and computer services, the department said.

In the industrial sector, which has been showing signs of strength lately, the number of manufacturing jobs rose by 25,000 in August as auto plants geared up for the new model year. In July the number of factory jobs fell by 27,000.

The department's survey of households showed that the number of jobless workers fell by 467,000 last month to 6.8 million, while those with jobs rose by 171,000 to 127.1 million. The civilian labour force -- employed workers and those seeking jobs -- fell by 296,000 to 133.9 million.
